stories.headline: Eight-vehicle I-70 crash near Georgetown involving Clear Creek deputies closes eastbound lanes, injures several
stories.summary:
A multi-vehicle crash on eastbound Interstate 70 near Georgetown shut down travel through the mountains on Thursday. The collision occurred around 11:25 a.m. and involved between eight and 10 vehicles, according to differing reports. The Denver Post reported eight people were injured, while the Denver Gazette cited six hospitalized, with some reports suggesting as many as nine.

According to Colorado State Patrol, Clear Creek County deputies were assisting a motorist with a semitrailer that may have been on fire when another vehicle struck three deputy patrol vehicles. That vehicle then crashed into four more vehicles and a second semitrailer. Three deputies were inside the patrol vehicles; two were taken to a hospital, one with possible injuries and one as a precaution. One motorist was airlifted by Flight for Life with serious injuries, and three others went by ambulance.

Eastbound I-70 was initially closed at mile marker 228 and the closure was later extended to Silverthorne at mile marker 205. CDOT advised detours via CO 9 to US 40 or US 285, and Loveland Pass was also closed, forcing long detours for skiers returning from Arapahoe Basin. No reopening time had been given.

stories.headline: Federal report details what went wrong in Knowles and Snyder fires that killed four firefighters
stories.summary:
A 102-page Department of the Interior report released Thursday found that extreme fire behavior, strained communications, understaffing and gaps in aerial supervision contributed to the deaths of four federal firefighters in western Colorado in June. The firefighters were overtaken by the fast-growing Snyder fire near the Colorado-Utah border west of Grand Junction on June 27.

Emily Barker, 38, Nick Hutcherson, 27, and Sydney Watson, 27, died in the burnover. Nathan Matthews, 43, later died of his injuries on July 24, and a fifth firefighter was injured. The Snyder fire grew from three fires on about 60 acres to a 28,000-acre blaze, spreading more than seven miles in about three hours. A rescue helicopter could not land because of heavy smoke.

Investigators wrote that no single decision or system failure fully explains the outcome, citing the cumulative effects of known limitations. The report points to areas where the new U.S. Wildland Fire Service can improve communications, fire observation, airspace awareness and dispatch coordination. Hutcherson's mother said failures by the duty officer and others caused her son's death and demanded accountability.

stories.headline: Polis tells JBC Medicaid will consume all Amendment 87 revenue by 2030
stories.summary:
Gov. Jared Polis warned the Joint Budget Committee Thursday that all revenue from Colorado's new graduated income tax will be needed to cover Medicaid by 2030. Amendment 87 passed with 51% of the vote and is projected to raise about $2 billion in its first year, with some estimates reaching $2.7 billion. The money is directed to health care, K-12 education, higher education and child care.

Polis, who opposed the measure, said rising Medicaid costs could leave education and child care without the funding voters expected. Medicaid spending was about $16 billion last year, nearly 40% of the state budget, and federal changes under H.R. 1, inflation and expired COVID-era funding will push costs higher.

His budget proposes a 4.3% increase in Medicaid spending, about $250 million, while cutting more than $600 million from projected costs. Lawmakers begin the 2027 session facing a $1.58 billion general fund shortfall, about $440 million of it tied to Medicaid. Polis said spending above his proposal would require cuts elsewhere in the budget.

stories.headline: Gov. Polis pardons 27 people convicted of minor crimes
stories.summary:
Gov. Jared Polis granted pardons to 27 people Thursday, all for relatively minor offenses, as he nears the end of his tenure as Colorado's governor. The governor's office released the list of names, which includes Victor Arellano, Richard Batdorf, Timothy Cordova and Luis Day, among others.

A pardon forgives a conviction and can remove barriers to employment, housing and other opportunities for those who received them. Polis has used his clemency power periodically during his time in office.

The pardons come as his term winds down following the November elections.

stories.headline: Democrats gather in Denver for 'What's Next' conference after midterm gains
stories.summary:
Democratic officials and strategists converged on Denver Thursday for the two-day "What's Next" conference hosted by Majority Democrats, days after what organizers called the party's best electoral performance in half a century. Denver Mayor Mike Johnston opened the event, saying "America tried on hate, and it didn't fit."

Democrats now hold majorities in both chambers of Congress and control at least 12 new state legislative chambers. In Colorado, they secured a legislative supermajority and are poised to win all but one congressional seat, though conservative ballot questions on transgender issues and crime also won approval.

Speakers include Sen.-elect James Talarico, Sen.-elect Josh Turek, Pete Buttigieg, Cory Booker, Josh Shapiro and likely House speaker Hakeem Jeffries. The gathering also serves as a showcase for Denver, which is seeking the 2028 Democratic National Convention.

stories.headline: DPS board votes 4-2 to close Robert F. Smith STEAM Academy
stories.summary:
The Denver Public Schools Board of Education voted 4-2 Thursday to close Robert F. Smith STEAM Academy at the end of the 2026-27 school year, five years after it opened. Superintendent Alex Marrero recommended the closure in October, citing enrollment that fell from 135 students to 24 over four years.

The school opened in 2021 with a model inspired by historically Black colleges and universities, and nearly 70% of its students have been Black. It had no enrollment boundary, so all students chose to attend. It moved buildings in 2023 but lacked amenities such as a sports field or auditorium that families had been promised.

DPS policy requires four years between enrollment-based closure rounds, and the district closed seven schools in 2025. The board used an operational closure, which is allowed at any time when per-student funding makes a school unsustainable. Board member Amy Klein Molk called it a very hard decision.

stories.headline: CDOT pauses full Colorado Boulevard bus rapid transit review until 2028
stories.summary:
The Colorado Department of Transportation is delaying a full bus rapid transit review of Colorado Boulevard until 2028 and will focus on sidewalks, intersections and other safety improvements in the meantime. The department said additional BRT features would benefit from performance data from other corridors, including Colfax Avenue. A center-running bus configuration was ruled inappropriate for the road.

The corridor runs roughly from I-70 and East 40th Avenue south to the Southmoor Station area. Neighborhood groups in Park Hill, Hilltop and Cherry Creek North, along with Glendale, have raised concerns about congestion and traffic diversion. About 19 neighborhood associations signed a resolution seeking a pause of at least two years after Colfax is finished.

Center-running lanes on East Colfax opened to buses in late September, with full Lynx BRT service targeted for early 2028. On Federal Boulevard, CDOT secured a $50 million commitment for stations, with construction expected in fall 2027. A citizen-led forum on the Colorado Boulevard plan was set for Thursday in Glendale.

stories.headline: RTD study finds agency generates $3.7 billion in economic and community impact
stories.summary:
A new economic impact study commissioned by the Regional Transportation District finds the agency is a major contributor to the metro Denver economy. It estimates RTD supports about 17,500 jobs and generates roughly $2.1 billion in annual economic activity.

The study also estimates about $1.6 billion each year in community and mobility benefits, for a combined total of about $3.7 billion. It concludes the agency produces $2.42 in economic value for every dollar invested.

The report arrives as Ballot Issue 7A, which would expand passenger rail across metro Denver and the Front Range through a sales tax, is part of the regional transit conversation.

stories.headline: Aurora Fire Rescue offers $60,000 reward in 2023 arson case
stories.summary:
Aurora Fire Rescue is offering a $60,000 reward for information that helps solve an arson that occurred around midnight in December 2023. The department is seeking tips from the public as the case remains unsolved.

Authorities have not released additional details in the available report. Anyone with information is encouraged to contact Aurora fire investigators.

stories.headline: Avalanche lose MacKinnon and Cale Makar to lower-body injuries in overtime loss at Ottawa
stories.summary:
Colorado lost both Nathan MacKinnon and Cale Makar to lower-body injuries in the second period of a 4-3 overtime loss to the Ottawa Senators on Thursday. MacKinnon appeared to suffer a midsection or hip injury, and the team's availability updates remain pending.

The Avalanche overcame a 2-0 deficit to force overtime and earned a point. Captain Gabe Landeskog said the team plays with whoever is healthy and hoped both players would be fine.

MacKinnon had 10 goals and 30 points entering the game, and Makar had five goals and 23 points. Colorado next plays Saturday against the Montreal Canadiens.

stories.headline: Rockies leave door open for Kyle Freeland reunion in free agency
stories.summary:
Colorado Rockies president of baseball operations Paul DePodesta said Tuesday the club has not ruled out bringing back left-hander Kyle Freeland, who became a free agent after the 2026 season. DePodesta said Freeland has done a lot for the organization.

Freeland, a Denver native, finished 2026 with a 4-12 record and a 6.65 ERA over 135 1/3 innings, after a 4.98 ERA in 2025. He finished fourth in 2018 National League Cy Young voting and started the wild-card game that season.

The Rockies finished 58-104, last in MLB, and are in a rebuilding offseason. Any reunion would likely come on a modest contract with competition for a rotation spot.

stories.headline: Nuggets at 6-4 as Aaron Gordon's slow start draws concern
stories.summary:
The Denver Nuggets improved to 6-4 with a road win over Memphis, but sit tenth in the Western Conference. Jamal Murray and Nikola Jokic have played at a high level while the rest of the roster has been slower to settle in.

Aaron Gordon scored nine points on 3-of-11 shooting in Wednesday's win. Through ten games he averages 11.0 points and 5.0 rebounds, shooting 38% from the field and 25.6% from three-point range.

Gordon missed 31 games in 2024-25 and 46 in 2025-26. Denver is expected to give him time to recover form, with Cameron Johnson among those who could pick up slack.

topStory.headline: Lutnick Agrees to Testify Before Senate Banking Committee as Bipartisan Scrutiny of Nvidia Grows After CEO Huang Resigns
topStory.summary:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick agreed Thursday to appear voluntarily before the Senate Banking Committee to answer questions about national security concerns tied to Nvidia. The announcement followed letters sent Thursday by committee chair Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., to Lutnick and Jensen Huang, who resigned earlier that day as Nvidia's chief executive. Scott asked Huang to testify on Dec. 3 and Lutnick on Dec. 10, and said the committee could issue a subpoena to Huang if he does not appear voluntarily. A Lutnick spokesperson, Kristen Eichamer, said the secretary had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily." Representatives for Huang did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the letter.

The inquiry follows reporting by The New York Times that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a top executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. U.S. intelligence agencies believe she was recruited by China's main spy agency. The revelations have added to concerns that Nvidia chips may have been smuggled or illegally accessed by Chinese AI companies. Nvidia has said it complies with U.S. export laws. Huang has hired lawyers who previously represented executives in government investigations, according to people familiar with the matter, and House Republicans said they are in discussions with him about testifying before other committees.

Lawmakers from both parties pressed for answers. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Lutnick should appear voluntarily but "may need to be subpoenaed" otherwise, and asked whether export controls were relaxed. Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., said he wanted Lutnick to testify "ASAP" and cited chips being exported in apparent defiance of President Trump's orders. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said Lutnick should testify without a subpoena. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called on Congress to "demand answers" from Huang and on the administration to explain its response once it learned of the relationship. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., the committee's top Democrat, said Huang's resignation "does not absolve him, other executives or the company" of responsibility, and urged officials to close export control loopholes. The top Democrats on two congressional committees also wrote to Lutnick saying they were investigating.

The Times reported that Lutnick has clashed with other senior administration officials over the past year on how to regulate advanced technology sales to Asia, particularly Nvidia's. Most senior officials favor tighter controls on advanced chips to keep China from closing the gap in AI, while critics in the administration and Congress say Commerce has become too close to Nvidia and failed to adequately police its sales to China. Current and former officials said Nvidia receives distinct treatment within the department, with its issues prioritized and routed through specific channels, and that Lutnick frequently speaks with Huang and hosts private meetings in his office. Commerce was also required to review companies for national security risks before the administration allowed Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China last year.

The White House has defended Lutnick, saying the president "maintains complete confidence in the secretary." The hearings, scheduled for December, will put the Commerce Department's role in issuing and enforcing export controls under public scrutiny, in a debate over whether selling advanced chips to China speeds its AI and military development or helps U.S. technology maintain global leadership. Scott wrote that Lutnick's testimony would be "essential" to the committee's oversight of those efforts. Whether Huang agrees to appear, and whether subpoenas become necessary, remain open questions.
